concepts.label: Nationalism and the Anti-Colonial Movement in India
concepts.cardText: In India, as in many other colonies, the growth of modern nationalism is intimately connected to the anti-colonial movement. People began discovering their unity in the process of their struggle with colonialism, and the sense of being oppressed under colonialism provided a shared bond that tied many different groups together. But each class and group felt the effects of colonialism differently, their experiences were varied and their notions of freedom were not always the same. The Congress under Mahatma Gandhi tried to forge these groups together within one movement, but the unity did not emerge without conflict.

concepts.label: The First World War and Hardship in India
concepts.cardText: The First World War created a new economic and political situation. A huge increase in defence expenditure was financed by war loans and increasing taxes: customs duties were raised and income tax introduced. Prices doubled between 1913 and 1918, causing extreme hardship for the common people. Villages were called upon to supply soldiers, and forced recruitment in rural areas caused widespread anger. In 1918-19 and 1920-21 crops failed, resulting in acute food shortages, accompanied by an influenza epidemic; according to the 1921 census, 12 to 13 million people perished. People hoped their hardships would end after the war, but that did not happen.

concepts.label: The Idea of Satyagraha
concepts.cardText: Mahatma Gandhi returned to India in January 1915 from South Africa, where he had successfully fought the racist regime with a novel method of mass agitation which he called satyagraha. The idea of satyagraha emphasised the power of truth and the need to search for truth. If the cause was true and the struggle was against injustice, physical force was not necessary to fight the oppressor. Without seeking vengeance or being aggressive, a satyagrahi could win the battle through non-violence by appealing to the conscience of the oppressor. Gandhi believed this dharma of non-violence could unite all Indians. In India he organised satyagraha in Champaran in 1917 against the oppressive plantation system, in Ahmedabad in 1918 among cotton mill workers, and in Kheda in 1918 to support peasants who could not pay revenue after crop failure and plague.

concepts.label: The Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh
concepts.cardText: In 1919 Gandhi decided to launch a nationwide satyagraha against the proposed Rowlatt Act, hurriedly passed through the Imperial Legislative Council despite the united opposition of Indian members. It gave the government enormous powers to repress political activities and allowed detention of political prisoners without trial for two years. Gandhi wanted non-violent civil disobedience, starting with a hartal on 6 April. On 10 April the police in Amritsar fired on a peaceful procession, provoking attacks on banks, post offices and railway stations; martial law was imposed and General Dyer took command. On 13 April at Jallianwalla Bagh, Dyer blocked the exit points of an enclosed ground and opened fire on a crowd, killing hundreds, to produce a moral effect. The government responded with brutal repression, and seeing violence spread, Gandhi called off the movement.

concepts.topicTitle: The First World War, Khilafat and Non-Cooperation
concepts.label: The Khilafat Issue
concepts.cardText: The Rowlatt satyagraha had been widespread but was limited mostly to cities and towns. Gandhi now felt the need to launch a more broad-based movement, but was certain it could not be organised without bringing Hindus and Muslims closer together. One way of doing this was to take up the Khilafat issue. The First World War had ended with the defeat of Ottoman Turkey, and there were rumours that a harsh peace treaty would be imposed on the Ottoman emperor, the Khalifa, the spiritual head of the Islamic world. To defend the Khalifa's temporal powers, a Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March 1919. Gandhi saw this as an opportunity to bring Muslims under the umbrella of a unified national movement, and at the Calcutta session of the Congress in September 1920 he convinced other leaders to start a non-cooperation movement in support of Khilafat as well as for swaraj.

concepts.label: Why Non-Cooperation?
concepts.cardText: In his book Hind Swaraj (1909) Gandhi declared that British rule was established in India with the cooperation of Indians and had survived only because of this cooperation. If Indians refused to cooperate, British rule would collapse within a year and swaraj would come. He proposed that the movement unfold in stages: first the surrender of titles awarded by the government and a boycott of civil services, army, police, courts, legislative councils, schools and foreign goods, and then, if the government used repression, a full civil disobedience campaign. Many in the Congress were reluctant to boycott the council elections of November 1920 and feared popular violence; after an intense tussle, a compromise at the Nagpur session in December 1920 adopted the Non-Cooperation programme.

concepts.label: The Movement in the Towns
concepts.cardText: The Non-Cooperation-Khilafat Movement began in January 1921, and various social groups participated, each with its own aspiration; all responded to the call of Swaraj, but the term meant different things to different people. In the towns the movement started with middle-class participation: thousands of students left government schools and colleges, headmasters and teachers resigned, lawyers gave up legal practice, and the council elections were boycotted in most provinces except Madras, where the Justice Party entered the council to gain some power. Foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops picketed and foreign cloth burnt; the import of foreign cloth halved between 1921 and 1922. The movement in the cities gradually slowed down because khadi cloth was more expensive than mill cloth and alternative Indian institutions were slow to come up, so students, teachers and lawyers trickled back.

concepts.label: Rebellion in the Countryside: Awadh
concepts.cardText: From the cities, the Non-Cooperation Movement spread to the countryside, drawing in the struggles of peasants and tribals. In Awadh, peasants were led by Baba Ramchandra, a sanyasi who had been to Fiji as an indentured labourer. The movement was against talukdars and landlords who demanded exorbitantly high rents and cesses, and forced peasants to do begar. The peasants demanded reduction of revenue, abolition of begar and social boycott of oppressive landlords; panchayats organised nai-dhobi bandhs to deprive landlords of barbers and washermen. The Oudh Kisan Sabha was set up in October 1920 headed by Jawaharlal Nehru and Baba Ramchandra. The Congress wanted to integrate the Awadh struggle into the wider movement, but the peasant movement developed in forms the leadership disliked: houses of talukdars were attacked, bazaars looted, and local leaders claimed Gandhi had said no taxes were to be paid and land redistributed.

concepts.label: Tribal Peasants and the Gudem Hills
concepts.cardText: Tribal peasants interpreted Gandhi's message and the idea of swaraj in yet another way. In the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh a militant guerrilla movement spread in the early 1920s, which the Congress could not approve. The colonial government had closed large forest areas, preventing people from entering the forests to graze cattle or collect fuelwood and fruits, which enraged the hill people because their livelihoods and traditional rights were denied; when the government forced them to contribute begar for road building, they revolted. Alluri Sitaram Raju led them. He claimed special powers, talked of Gandhi's greatness and urged khadi and giving up drinking, yet asserted that India could be liberated only by force, not non-violence. The rebels attacked police stations and carried on guerrilla warfare for swaraj; Raju was captured and executed in 1924 and became a folk hero.

concepts.label: Swaraj in the Plantations
concepts.cardText: For plantation workers in Assam, freedom meant the right to move freely in and out of the confined space in which they were enclosed, and retaining a link with the village from which they had come. Under the Inland Emigration Act of 1859 workers were not permitted to leave the tea gardens without permission, which was rarely given. When they heard of the Non-Cooperation Movement, thousands defied the authorities, left the plantations and headed home, believing Gandhi Raj was coming and everyone would be given land in their own villages. They never reached their destination: stranded by a railway and steamer strike, they were caught by the police and brutally beaten up. concepts.label: Chauri Chaura and the End of Non-Cooperation
concepts.cardText: At Chauri Chaura in Gorakhpur, a peaceful demonstration in a bazaar turned into a violent clash with the police. concepts.label: Depression, the Simon Commission and Purna Swaraj
concepts.cardText: Two factors shaped Indian politics towards the late 1920s. The worldwide economic depression made agricultural prices fall from 1926 and collapse after 1930; peasants found it difficult to sell their harvests and pay revenue, and by 1930 the countryside was in turmoil. The new Tory government in Britain constituted a Statutory Commission under Sir John Simon to look into the constitutional system in India, but it had no Indian member. When it arrived in 1928 it was greeted with the slogan 'Go back Simon', with all parties including the Congress and the Muslim League taking part. In October 1929 Lord Irwin announced a vague offer of dominion status and a Round Table Conference, which did not satisfy the Congress. In December 1929 under Jawaharlal Nehru the Lahore Congress formalised the demand of Purna Swaraj or full independence and declared that 26 January 1930 would be celebrated as Independence Day, but the celebrations attracted very little attention.

concepts.label: The Salt March
concepts.cardText: Mahatma Gandhi found in salt a powerful symbol that could unite the nation. On 31 January 1930 he sent Viceroy Irwin a letter stating eleven demands, some of general interest and some specific to different classes, so that all classes could identify with them. The most stirring was the demand to abolish the salt tax. Salt was consumed by the rich and poor alike and was one of the most essential items of food; the tax and the government monopoly over its production revealed the most oppressive face of British rule. The letter was an ultimatum: if the demands were not met by 11 March, the Congress would launch civil disobedience. Irwin was unwilling to negotiate, so Gandhi started the salt march with 78 volunteers over 240 miles from Sabarmati to Dandi, walking for 24 days. On 6 April he reached Dandi and ceremonially violated the law by manufacturing salt from boiling sea water.

concepts.label: The Civil Disobedience Movement and the Gandhi-Irwin Pact
concepts.cardText: The Civil Disobedience Movement differed from Non-Cooperation: people were now asked not only to refuse cooperation but also to break colonial laws. Thousands broke the salt law and demonstrated at government salt factories, foreign cloth was boycotted, liquor shops picketed, peasants refused to pay revenue and chaukidari taxes, village officials resigned and forest people violated forest laws. The government arrested Congress leaders one by one; after Abdul Ghaffar Khan's arrest in April 1930 angry crowds in Peshawar faced police firing, and when Gandhi was arrested industrial workers in Sholapur attacked symbols of British rule. About 100,000 people were arrested. Gandhi again called off the movement and entered into the Gandhi-Irwin Pact on 5 March 1931, agreeing to attend the Round Table Conference while the government agreed to release political prisoners. The negotiations in London broke down, repression resumed, Gandhi relaunched the movement, but by 1934 it lost its momentum.

concepts.label: Rich and Poor Peasants in Civil Disobedience
concepts.cardText: In the countryside, rich peasant communities like the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh were active in the movement. As producers of commercial crops they were very hard hit by the trade depression and falling prices, and could not pay the government's revenue demand when their cash income disappeared; the government refused to reduce the demand. For them the fight for swaraj was a struggle against high revenues, and they were deeply disappointed when the movement was called off in 1931 without the revenue rates being revised, so many refused to participate when it restarted in 1932. The poorer peasantry, many of them small tenants, wanted unpaid rent remitted and joined radical movements led by Socialists and Communists. The Congress, wary of upsetting rich peasants and landlords, was unwilling to support 'no rent' campaigns, so its relationship with poor peasants remained uncertain.

concepts.label: Business Classes and Industrial Workers
concepts.cardText: During the First World War Indian merchants and industrialists made huge profits and became powerful. Keen on expanding business, they reacted against colonial policies that restricted business activities, wanting protection against imports and a rupee-sterling exchange ratio that would discourage imports. They formed the Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress in 1920 and the FICCI in 1927, led by Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G. D. Birla, and supported Civil Disobedience at first with financial assistance and refusing to trade in imported goods. Most saw swaraj as a time when colonial restrictions on business would end. After the failure of the Round Table Conference they were no longer uniformly enthusiastic, fearing militant activities, prolonged disruption of business and the influence of socialism. Industrial workers took part in large numbers only in the Nagpur region; as industrialists came closer to the Congress, workers stayed aloof, though some adopted boycott in their own struggles. The Congress was reluctant to include workers' demands, feeling it would alienate industrialists and divide the anti-imperial forces.

concepts.label: Women in the Civil Disobedience Movement
concepts.cardText: Another important feature of the Civil Disobedience Movement was the large-scale participation of women. During the salt march thousands of women came out of their homes to listen to Gandhi. They participated in protest marches, manufactured salt, picketed foreign cloth and liquor shops, and many went to jail. In urban areas these women were from high-caste families; in rural areas they came from rich peasant households. Moved by Gandhi's call, they began to see service to the nation as a sacred duty of women. concepts.label: The Limits of Civil Disobedience: Dalits and the Poona Pact
concepts.cardText: Not all social groups were moved by the abstract concept of swaraj. The 'untouchables', who from around the 1930s began to call themselves dalit, had long been ignored by the Congress for fear of offending conservative high-caste sanatanis. Gandhi declared that swaraj would not come for a hundred years if untouchability was not eliminated; he called them harijan, organised satyagraha for their entry into temples and access to public wells, tanks, roads and schools, and cleaned toilets himself. But many dalit leaders wanted a different political solution: reserved seats in educational institutions and separate electorates, believing political empowerment would resolve their social disabilities. Dr B.R. Ambedkar, who organised the Depressed Classes Association in 1930, demanded separate electorates at the second Round Table Conference. When the British conceded, Gandhi began a fast unto death, believing separate electorates would slow their integration into society. Ambedkar accepted his position, and the Poona Pact of September 1932 gave the Depressed Classes reserved seats in provincial and central legislative councils, to be voted in by the general electorate.

concepts.label: Muslims and the Civil Disobedience Movement
concepts.cardText: Some Muslim political organisations were lukewarm in their response to Civil Disobedience. After the decline of the Non-Cooperation-Khilafat Movement a large section of Muslims felt alienated from the Congress. From the mid-1920s the Congress came to be more visibly associated with openly Hindu religious nationalist groups like the Hindu Mahasabha. As relations worsened, each community organised religious processions with militant fervour, provoking communal clashes and riots, and every riot deepened the distance between the communities. The Congress and the Muslim League tried to renegotiate an alliance in 1927, with the main differences over representation in future assemblies; Jinnah was willing to give up separate electorates if Muslims were assured reserved seats in the Central Assembly and proportional representation in Bengal and Punjab. All hope disappeared at the All Parties Conference in 1928 when M.R. Jayakar of the Hindu Mahasabha opposed compromise. By the time Civil Disobedience started there was suspicion and distrust, and many Muslims feared the culture and identity of minorities would be submerged under a Hindu majority.

concepts.cardText: Nationalism spreads when people begin to believe that they are all part of the same nation and discover some unity that binds them together. This sense of collective belonging came partly through the experience of united struggles, but there were also a variety of cultural processes through which nationalism captured people's imagination. History and fiction, folklore and songs, popular prints and symbols all played a part in the making of nationalism.

concepts.label: Bharat Mata
concepts.cardText: The identity of the nation is most often symbolised in a figure or image. It was in the twentieth century, with the growth of nationalism, that the identity of India came to be visually associated with the image of Bharat Mata. The image was first created by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, who in the 1870s wrote Vande Mataram as a hymn to the motherland; it was later included in his novel Anandamath and widely sung during the Swadeshi movement in Bengal. Moved by the Swadeshi movement, Abanindranath Tagore painted his famous image of Bharat Mata as an ascetic figure, calm, composed, divine and spiritual. The image later acquired many forms in popular prints, and devotion to this mother figure came to be seen as evidence of one's nationalism.

concepts.label: Folklore, Flags and Reinterpretation of History
concepts.cardText: Ideas of nationalism also developed through a movement to revive Indian folklore. In the late nineteenth century nationalists began recording folk tales sung by bards and toured villages to gather folk songs and legends, believing they gave a true picture of traditional culture that outside forces had damaged; preserving the folk tradition was essential to discover one's national identity and restore pride in the past. Rabindranath Tagore collected ballads, nursery rhymes and myths in Bengal, and Natesa Sastri published a four-volume collection of Tamil folk tales in Madras. Leaders became aware of icons and symbols: during the Swadeshi movement a tricolour flag with eight lotuses and a crescent moon was designed, and by 1921 Gandhi had designed the Swaraj flag, a tricolour with a spinning wheel representing self-help. Indians also reinterpreted history to counter the British view that they were backward and primitive, looking to the glorious achievements of ancient times followed by decline under colonisation. But glorifying a Hindu past and Hindu iconography left people of other communities feeling left out.

concepts.topicTitle: Conclusion and the Quit India Movement
concepts.label: A Nation with Many Voices
concepts.cardText: A growing anger against the colonial government was bringing together various groups and classes of Indians into a common struggle for freedom in the first half of the twentieth century. The Congress under Mahatma Gandhi tried to channel people's grievances into organised movements for independence and to forge national unity. But diverse groups participated with varied aspirations and expectations, and as their grievances were wide-ranging, freedom from colonial rule meant different things to different people. The Congress continuously attempted to resolve differences and ensure that the demands of one group did not alienate another, which is precisely why the unity within the movement often broke down. The high points of nationalist unity were followed by phases of disunity and inner conflict; what was emerging was a nation with many voices wanting freedom from colonial rule.

concepts.topicTitle: Conclusion and the Quit India Movement
concepts.label: Quit India Movement
concepts.cardText: The failure of the Cripps Mission and the effects of World War II created widespread discontentment in India. This led Gandhi to launch a movement calling for complete withdrawal of the British from India. The Congress Working Committee, meeting in Wardha on 14 July 1942, passed the historic Quit India resolution demanding the immediate transfer of power to Indians. On 8 August 1942 in Bombay, the All India Congress Committee endorsed the resolution, which called for a non-violent mass struggle on the widest possible scale, and Gandhi delivered the famous Do or Die speech. The movement almost brought the state machinery to a standstill in large parts of the country, with students, workers and peasants and leaders and women participating. The British responded with much force, yet it took more than a year to suppress the movement.
